Obaidul Hamid2 · Ian Hardy2 Received: 19 October 2024 / Accepted: 25 November 2025 © The Author(s) 2025 Abstract Although contemporary language-in-education policy (LEP) in developing societies often represents English as a panacea for poverty and a key tool for empowering people from socioeconomic disadvantage, not much is known about how this de- velopment potential unfolds for disenfranchised people. Motivated by social justice, and drawing on a framework that construes development as an ideology and utilises social theories from Pierre Bourdieu, Michel Foucault, and Sara Ahmed, this ar- ticle interrogates how English-in-education for individual and social development relates to students and parents in low socioeconomic status contexts. We focus on one school located in such a context in Bangladesh, and engage with the school principal, English teachers, parents, and students using interview and focus group discussion. Thematic analysis of the data reveals that while English-in-education policy creates neoliberal subjectivities among students and parents in relation to a transformative social imaginary and better economic futures, LEP misrecognis- es how the acquisition of the linguistic capital of English is conditioned by their human and social experiences of living. We highlight how education, including English learning, is grounded in parents’ and students’ everyday life experiences and struggles, and argue that by misrecognising these key dimensions, LEP hides the systems of marginalisation and uneven provisions for linguistic human capital development. The study offers new perspectives to critique development ideology in relation to LEP and contributes to language policy around the United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goals for inclusive and equitable provision for language education to ensure inclusive social development in developing societies. Introduction Human capital development dominates English-in-education policy goals in devel- oping societies as part of a broader development agenda shaped by neoliberalism (Ali & Hamid, 2020; Price, 2014). As a political and economic rationality, neoliberalism re-configures the governance of populations by emphasising state deregulation, pri- vatisation, and individualisation to align all aspects of social, cultural, and economic life with the logics of the market (Harvey, 2005). As the linguistic capital of Eng- lish is viewed as a necessary part of human capital in a neoliberal world, invest- ment in English language education is considered an investment in human capital development (Ali et al., 2023b). Specifically, English-in-education policy is guided by human capital theory (HCT) in a neoliberal environment, which assumes that everyone has an equal chance of acquiring skills and competencies and developing their employability potential. English-in-education for human capital development comes with the promise of double benefits: individual (micro-level) social mobility through employability and income, and national (macro-level) development through individuals’ productivity and contribution to the economy. Although this agenda takes a rather narrow, exclusively economic view of development in language-in- education policy (LEP), human capital development seems to have become a priority for macro-level policy makers (Erling, 2017). More recently, human capital development in LEP has been linked to the United Nations’ (UN) Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) (Coleman, 2017). A notable example is provided by a £50 million British government funded development aid project called English in Action (2008–2017), which was implemented in Bangladesh to help Bangladeshis develop their English language proficiency to become employ- able and take the nation out of poverty (Ali et al., 2023a). Drawing on HCT, the ELT aid intervention was linked to SDGs as it was believed to provide an opportunity for disenfranchised people to develop proficiency in English en route to employment and economic development (Eyres et al., 2019). This aid project illustrates how the human capital orientation to language policy presents English and language teaching as key tools for inclusive social development—hence, English for everyone. HCT, however, has been critiqued as it ignores structural issues that underpin social prac- tices including schooling (Ali & Hamid, 2024a; Marginson, 2017). This critique has purchase for the human capital orientation to LEP as structural issues have also been reported in language education (see Block, 2013; Terasawa, 2016). As valued capital, language and education contribute to creating ‘winners’ and ‘losers’ in society (Ali et al., 2020), giving nation-states an opportunity to use them as tools for governing citizens (Gillies, 2008; Flores, 2020). These governmental rationalities are informed by the neoliberal principle of individualisation and the dis- course of meritocracy which create specific subjectivities among people who will act upon these resources for upward social mobility. However, as these governmental rationalities promote individualisation, success/failure in learning English becomes a matter of individual effort and hard work (Highet & Del Percio, 2021), leaving dis- enfranchised people, particularly those in low socioeconomic status (SES) contexts, vulnerable (Batruch et al., 2023). Thus, when it comes to the question of English for everyone, we need to examine how these discourses of English and development relate to disenfranchised people and how their acquisition of the linguistic capital of English is influenced by their lived experiences. Although contemporary LEP often represents English as a panacea for poverty and a key tool for empowering people from socioeconomic disadvantage (Eyres et al., 2019), there is a dearth of literature around how this development potential relates to these people in relation to their human and social conditions that mediate language learning. By human and social conditions, we refer to people’s day-to-day living, influenced by their financial, educational, physical, and emotional circumstances. In this article, we address this gap and focus on a secondary school in a low SES context in Bangladesh to explore the following research questions: 1. How do key stakeholders affiliated with the school make sense of English in the context of development? 2. How do their sense-making and practices of the development of linguistic human capital relate to students’ and parents’ human and social conditions of living? To explore these questions, we construct a framework which construes development as an ideology and draws on social theories from Pierre Bourdieu, Michel Foucault, and Sara Ahmed to illustrate how the development foci in LEP are not neutral but ideologically motivated by neoliberal governmental rationalities. The framework proves useful in relation to our social justice agenda which focused on unpacking injustice; we elaborate this in the Discussion section. The methodology section outlines the research design, participant recruitment, data col- lection and analysis. The conceptual framework The conceptual framework developed for the present study is hybrid in nature which brings together understandings of development and relevant theoretical resources provided by Bourdieu, Foucault and Sarah Ahmed. This section outlines each com- ponent of this framework. Development as ideology Development is a contested term. According to Slim (1995), ‘‘[d]evelopment is essen- tially about change: not just any change, but a definitive improvement—a change for better’’ (p. 143). During the 1950s and 1960s, development was measured in terms of national economic growth and GDP. This gave birth to the discipline of Develop- ment Economics during the second half of the twentieth century, focusing on how 1 3 1 Page 4 of 26 M. M. Ali et al. to transform developing nations from agriculture-based economies to industrialised market economies for poverty reduction. However, this approach appeared problem- atic as GDP growth did not necessarily bring about positive changes in people’s lives, but rather social inequalities and income gaps became widespread (Harber, 2014). Later, Amartya Sen shifted the focus of development towards human-centric factors, emphasising individuals’ freedom of choice, education, and health as key factors contributing to poverty reduction and social mobilities (Sen, 1999), which were then incorporated into the UN’s Human Development Index. However, Amartya Sen’s conceptualisation of development as freedom has been criticised as it depoliticises development by ‘‘his reluctance to focus on the sources of power in a society and how that power is reproduced’’ (Navarro, 2000, p. 666). Like HCT, Sen’s conceptualisation of development does not consider unequal social rela- tionships and structures which mediate people’s access to opportunities to achieve freedom. Critiquing Sen’s concept of development ‘‘as the expansion of freedom’’, Sandbrook (2000) argues that ‘‘the vast majority of poor and oppressed people do not, and will not, inhabit this idealised world’’ (p. 1072). In this paper, we take these issues into consideration and construe development as a deeply ideological construct (Li, 2007a). In that sense, development is a regime of ideologies and discourses which shapes what is construed as progressive and positive change (Rist & Shenton, 2019). Capital, governmentality, object of desire, and misrecognition In language policy research, scholars tend to use Bourdieu’s concepts of linguistic capital and Foucault’s governmentality separately. The present article shows how Bourdieu’s concepts of capital, field, and field logics may provide an initial framing to better understand Foucault’s governmentality. We also incorporate Sara Ahmed’s theory of ‘affective economies’ to illustrate how subjectivities and desires are gener- ated under governmental rationalities. The framework is further refined by bringing Bourdieu’s concept of misrecognition in dialogue with Foucault’s notion of discourse and Ahmed’s affective economies, making a theoretical contribution to language pol- icy research. Bourdieu conceptualised society as consisting of multiple autonomous spaces, which he termed ‘fields’. Each field is characterised by certain rules or logics which represent certain thoughts and behaviours as legitimate, while construing those not conforming to the logics of the field as illegitimate (Bourdieu, 1977). What is valued within a field is what Bourdieu calls capital. There are three forms of capital, namely economic capital (wealth), social capital (relations and networks), and cultural capi- tal (knowledge, skills, language proficiency, and academic qualifications) (Bourdieu, 1986). These forms of capital are relational, and they determine individuals’ positions within a social field—for example, more accumulated capital means a higher position within the field to access social and economic opportunities. Bourdieu’s theorising of field helps in understanding education as a field in which tastes and cultures of the powerful group in society are institutionalised as the legiti- mate goals of schooling (Bourdieu & Passeron, 1990). For example, languages pre- ferred in school become the legitimate subjects for everyone to learn and not learning these languages may disadvantage students in the education and employment market. 1 3 Governmental rationalities and misrecognising human and social… Page 5 of 26 1 Language proficiency works as ‘linguistic capital’ only if this is valued by people in power in the relevant field (Bourdieu, 1991). As linguistic capital is convertible into economic capital, it is also considered a form of human capital—or linguistic human capital, more precisely (Grin, 2003). Whether or not individuals acquire the linguistic human capital legitimised through LEP will have direct implications for their future employment prospects, income and mobility (Azam et al., 2013). Language as a form of human capital provides ‘technologies’ for the state to gov- ern people and regulate their thoughts and practices in a neoliberal environment (Del Percio & Wong, 2020; Urla, 2019). This is what Foucault calls governmentality—the process of governing people and disciplining their thoughts by creating conditions whereby they internalise governmental rationalities and learn to regulate their con- duct and behaviours (Foucault, 1991; Senellart & Foucault, 2008). Doherty (2007) posits that ‘‘the practice of government leads to consideration of the multitude of techniques, schemas, structures and ideas deliberately mobilised in attempting to direct or influence the conduct of others’’ (p. 196). For Foucault, ‘‘governmentality’s principal form of knowledge is political economy’’ (Li, 2007b, p. 277). This means that the very act of governing is informed by dominant economic philosophies, such as neoliberalism in our time (Block, 2017). Foucault, like Bourdieu, was mindful of the impact of neoliberalism on every aspect of social, political, and economic affairs since the 1970s. In a neoliberal environment, ‘‘government operates by educating desires and configuring habits, aspirations and beliefs’’ (Li, 2007b, p. 275). Neoliberal governmental rationalities have come to shape language policies and LEP across societies. For example, Flores’ (2013) study reveals how the national bilingual policy in the United States serves to manage the language behaviours of its citizens from a neoliberal perspective. In South Korea, Park (2011) examines how English has been framed in policy as a form of human capital for neoliberal govern- mentality; the purpose of such framing is to develop entrepreneurial subjects who would invest in English learning for self-improvement. These neoliberal governmen- tal rationalities have also manifested through policy artefacts such as textbooks (Bori & Block, 2024; Shah, 2025) and programme booklets (Warriner, 2016) which are targeted to develop individuals’ dispositions towards what is required by the broader political economy shaped by neoliberalism. In this context, English is associated with both pride and profit (Duchêne & Heller, 2012), generating desire among people for this form of linguistic human capital. De Costa et al., (2019) argue that the entrepreneurial subjectivity is linked with an affec- tive regime which creates a culture of self-management for language learning. In other words, neoliberal governmental rationalities in language policy are associated with a process of activating individuals’ affect and subjectivities, and thereby creat- ing ‘neoliberal subjects’ (Park, 2021). Park (2013) argues that ‘‘the ideal neoliberal subject does not begrudgingly participate in work, but displays initiative, responsi- bility, and flexibility, willing to take risks and engaging in projects of endless self- improvement…’’ (pp. 559–560). This willingness to take responsibility is activated by an affective regime promoted by neoliberalism (De Costa et al., 2019; Rojo & Del Percio, 2020). To make sense of the affective regime in language policy and LEP, we draw on Sara Ahmed’s theory of ‘affective economies’ to understand how people’s desires for 1 3 1 Page 6 of 26 M. M. Ali et al. English are generated through discursive practices. The concept of affective econo- mies refers to the mechanisms through which emotions are circulated using certain discourses so that they become part of the social order (Ahmed, 2014). Ahmed uses the metaphor of ‘stickiness’ and delineates how people’s emotions ‘stick’ to ideas and objects and how these ideas and objects become their object of desire (Ahmed, 2004, 2010). This concept has been applied to language policy research which shows how discourses around pride and profit generate desires for English whereby people associate English with upward social/career mobilities and development (see Highet, 2024; Salonga, 2022). Our data suggested that while the promises of English and education activate people’s affective desires and subjectivities for individual and social development, they hardly recognise social structures and conditions of marginalised people and thereby naturalise unequal social games (i.e., struggles over human capital develop- ment) through LEP and school curricula. Hence, we go beyond the current theoretical understanding of political economy in language policy research highlighted above. In this context, we found Bourdieu’s concept of misrecognition (Bourdieu & Passeron, 1990) helpful to extend the theoretical understanding of language policy research. Misrecognition refers to the process through which individuals construe arbitrary social norms, beliefs, practices, hierarchies, and power relations not as arbitrary structures but as neutral and unquestionable (Bourdieu, 2000). This process is sus- tained by their habitus, defined as durable dispositions developed through the amount of familial economic, social, and cultural capital accrued, as well as other life experi- ences (Bourdieu, 1984). Habitus predisposes individuals to comply with the logics of a social field, which determine which discourses are considered legitimate, and which are not, in that field (Bourdieu, 1977). At the same time, legitimacy is achieved because individuals internalise those logics and the discourses associated with them as part of their habitus; this all occurs through the process of misrecognition (Bour- dieu, 2000). In the context of LEP, misrecognition may operate through the process of language choices in which some languages are prioritised based on ideological and economic rationalities. This will place some students (particularly those coming from privileged backgrounds) in a better position because their language is chosen as the school subject, while disadvantaging others who need to learn the language of the powerful group (Vandrick, 2014). LEP misrecognises the structural barriers for students from marginalised backgrounds (Tollefson & Tsui, 2014). Nonetheless, misrecognition operates as hegemonic effects because of the complicity of the mar- ginalised themselves (Bourdieu & Passeron, 1990). Bourdieu’s concept of misrecog- nition provides an opportunity to problematise the human capital orientation to LEP and disrupt the generalised discourses of language and development by documenting how the acquisition of linguistic human capital is mediated by social structures, and the human and social conditions hiding social inequalities and injustices. 1 3 Governmental rationalities and misrecognising human and social… Page 7 of 26 1 Language policy in Bangladesh: development as ideology and English-in-education Bangladesh is a multilingual polity with over three dozen languages in the local lin- guistic ecology (Hamid & Ali, 2021). Language played a key role in the birth of Bangladesh as an independent nation in 1971, breaking away from the Federation of Pakistan. After the Partition of India in 1947, Urdu was proposed by the West Paki- stan leaders as the only official language of the newly formed decolonised nation. This not only upset the East Pakistani population who outnumbered those in West Pakistan but also created a sense of linguistic nationalism centring Bangla which culminated through a nine month-long liberation war in 1971, resulting in a new nation-state (Bangladesh). The language policy of the newly independent country was dominated by Bangla nationalism, which supressed all other languages. Ban- gla was adopted as the national language while English—the ex-colonial language of power and prestige—was demoted in all domains including education. Bangla was considered essential for national identity, unity, and workforce development for nation-building. These dominant ideologies also reflected in the language-in-educa- tion policy, emphasising Bangla as the medium of instruction. The nationalistic euphoria, however, appeared problematic for Bangladesh’s inte- gration with the global economy. Therefore, during the 1990s, Bangladesh’s public policies redefined national development reflecting more neoliberal ideologies and an overt emphasis on human capital development as the primary means of national economic growth (Muhammad, 2021). Hence, development in this context needs to be seen from an ideological perspective as new governmental rationalities emerged in a neoliberal climate. These rationalities were also reflected in language policy which enacted the neoliberalistion of English language education, where English was recognised as a form of human capital and a key tool for national development (Ali & Hamid, 2022). English was introduced as a compulsory school subject for Years 1–12. While primary and secondary education are provided through Bangla or Eng- lish medium depending on the stream of education, higher education institutions have predominantly shifted towards English medium instruction in the private sector in particular, reflecting neoliberal governmental rationalities. Importantly, the broader development context of Bangladesh, underpinned by neoliberal ideologies, has compromised the national policy sovereignty as Bangla- desh needed to depend on foreign aid and the expertise of development partners to neoliberalise language education policy. This not only paved the way for local- global partnerships in ELT policy reforms since the 1990s but also opened a window for an ideological regime of development to shape discourses about what counts as relevant language in relation to the employment market (Ali & Hamid, 2022). As previously mentioned in the Introduction, the English in Action mega-project was funded by the UK government’s Department for International Development (DFID) and implemented through a consortium of three international organisations (Mott MacDonald, BBC Media Action, and The Open University, UK) and two local NGOs (‘Underprivileged Children’s Educational Programme’ [UCEP] and ‘Friends in Vil- lage Development Bangladesh’ [FIVDB]). The project aimed to ‘‘contribute to the economic development in Bangladesh by providing English as a tool for better access 1 3 1 Page 8 of 26 M. M. Ali et al. to the world economy’’ (English in Action, n.d.). English in Action had two com- ponents: School Initiative and Media and Adult Learning Initiative. Activities for School Initiative included training for primary and secondary school teachers and developing digital materials aligning with the government prescribed textbooks. The Media and Adult Learning Initiative aimed to ‘‘reduce barriers and improve percep- tion of English learning’’ and ‘‘provide accessible, affordable English language learn- ing materials’’ by creating an initiative called BBC Janala (‘Janala’ meaning window) (English in Action, n.d.). To achieve these goals, BBC Janala used multi-platforms including television programmes, mobile phones, English clubs, audio CDs, and print media to reach a wider population. Reflecting neoliberal governmental rationalities, these initiatives provided mechanisms for shaping people’s dispositions around the economic value of English and how they are associated with better economic futures. In that sense, English in Action as development aid is not just a technical support, it is a form of neoliberal governmentality operationalising mechanisms which shape peoples’ dispositions and desires for the linguistic capital of English. Methodology The study and the research context We employed a qualitative case study (Silverman, 2013) to examine how English-in- education policy for human capital development unfolded in a Bangladeshi secondary school located in a low SES context. We adopted a critical realist paradigm (Bhaskar, 1975), which emphasises that ‘reality’ can exist independently from our perceptions and beliefs but that such ‘reality’ cannot be typically ‘seen’ or ‘observed’ as it exists as deep and hidden structures. This ontological positionality aligns with our theo- retical framework which recognises invisible logics of the field (Bourdieu), govern- mental rationalities underpinning policy (Foucault) and emotions in action (Ahmed). This ontological position guided our epistemology manifest in critically interrogat- ing development ideologies in relation to LEP. Ethics approval was obtained for the research from the University of Queensland and all ethics rules and guidelines were followed in engaging with the participants, ensuring informed consent, respect, pri- vacy, confidentiality and anonymity. Our analysis reveals a concerning picture. While language-in-education policy and broader education pro- visions create a so-called meritocratic system of governance, they seem to misrec- ognise the very social structures—including parental cultural and economic capital that mark social class status and shape both parents’ and children’s human and social condition of living—that underpin educational practices and inequalities. However, such a culture of individualisation of failure adds to further hardships of these marginalised people by misrecognising how such a climate may help school and government to avoid taking responsibility for ensuring inclusive education. Discussion and implications: governing the misrecognition of English-in-education policy The findings reported in this article contribute to understanding how state-level lan- guage and education provision for human capital development relates to people and their wellbeing in low SES contexts. For LEP research, the findings highlight the importance of subjecting the broader development ideologies and the promises of English generated through aid-based projects such as English in Action to critical scrutiny. They also emphasise the need for recognising people’s human and social conditions and their lived experiences in the context of dominant discourses about linguistic capital accumulation and education as key tools for individual mobility and social development. To the best of our knowledge, such relationships have not received adequate attention in LEP research (see Block, 2018 for a critique of how language policy research has given inadequate attention to such relationships). Our findings suggest that development ideologies promoted by LEP and aid-based proj- ects such as English in Action in Bangladesh promote neoliberal governmentality as a way of creating desire among people for what is conceived as human capital development. These governmental rationalities reflect a neoliberal way of manag- ing populations for economic growth, whereby national development is inextricably linked with individuals’ development (Li, 2007a). These assumptions underpinning broader development agenda mean that development in LEP and aid-based projects is not a neutral process but needs to be seen from an ideological perspective (Ali et al., 2023a). Reflecting this ideological perspective, what is notable in our analysis is the con- nections that the parents and students made between education and their human and social conditions of living. The parents, for example, linked their poor human and social conditions to their lack of knowledge and skills (i.e., human capital), reflecting the workings of neoliberal governmentality and human capital theory (Del Percio & Wong, 2020). Their challenging human and social experiences of life created in them a strong affective drive in relation to their children’s education and future; they did not want their children to be subjected to the same experiences when they grew up. In this context, linguistic capital and education become their ‘objects of desire’ and symbols of future happiness and hope for emancipation from poverty and hardship (Highet, 2024). However, the students’ experiences of poverty, hunger, and their sub- 1 3 1 Page 20 of 26 M. M. Ali et al. optimal human and social conditions already mean that their condition is very similar to their parents. Importantly, acquisition of linguistic human capital is implicated in parental and students’ human and social conditions of living. These findings add to the existing literature in language policy that highlights governmental rationalities and affective regimes in English language learning and language education in devel- opment contexts (e.g., De Costa et al., 2019; Highet, 2024; Park, 2011; Rojo & Del Percio, 2020; Salonga, 2022; Shah, 2025; Warriner, 2016). Our analysis has highlighted that social structures in the form of socioeconomic stratification and social class dispositions marked by individuals’ economic and cul- tural capital mediate access to the linguistic capital of English, and the quality of this experience. Reflecting these structures, it appears that teachers, parents, and students from low SES contexts run an uneven and inequitable race, sustained by inadequate economic, material, and linguistic resources. This is a stifling situation created by the state’s LEP policy that has introduced English for everyone with the assumption that it will benefit everybody. However, such policy has misrecognised the social structures which influence human and social capital development. More broadly, these findings mean that contrary to the discourses of development, misrecognition of social struc- tures and how they inform language learning and education, LEP and development aid may contribute to perpetuating social inequalities by failing to ensure inclusive and equitable human capital distribution processes in society, thereby simply exacer- bating existing divides. Our combined framework of social theories proved useful in exploring LEP from a social justice perspective by unpacking how injustice may be disguised under devel- opment discourses in LEP. We understand justice ‘‘as the overcoming of injustice’’ (Fraser, 2012 as cited in Piller, 2021, p. 1). In the present context, such justice in LEP and language education may be achieved by addressing marginalised human and social conditions and learning experiences caused by misrecognition and the normalisation of unequal linguistic human capital development. Our framework con- tributes to the social justice agenda in relation to language policy and education for human capital development by unpacking how misrecognition operates through gov- ernmental rationalities and dispositions shaped by development ideologies. This is the first step towards ‘‘the promotion of an understanding that it is the responsibility of institutions to ensure equitable access [and provision for equitable human capital development], rather than the responsibility of [only] individuals’’ (Piller, 2021, p. 5). The findings reported in this article have policy and theoretical implications. From a policy perspective, they highlight how LEP may relate to the UN’s SDG4 (Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportu- nities for all) and SDG8 (Promote sustained,inclusive and sustainable economic growth,full and productive employment and decent work for all). Our findings indicate that the acquisition of linguistic human capital would not be inclusive and equitable if LEP misrecognises how social structures and people’s human and social conditions affect human capital development. The moral imperative and emotional labour of accumulating capital on the one hand, and the struggles, hardship and misrecogni- tion of unequal social structures on the other, result in a form of symbolic violence, where inequalities are normalised through the discourses of development (Bourdieu, 1991). As such, governmental rationalities based on ‘hard work’ and meritocracy 1 3 Governmental rationalities and misrecognising human and social… Page 21 of 26 1 become problematic. The distribution of human capital needs to be inclusive and equitable, reflecting people’s human and social conditions and everyday lived experi- ences. Importantly, inequitable linguistic human capital distribution would not just fail in relation to students’ education provision (SDG4); it would also have broader implications in terms of students’ future employment (SDG8), working against the goals for inclusive social development. The role of English in employment is undeni- able (Azam et al., 2013). Hence, students from low SES contexts are likely to be dis- advantaged in the competitive employment field if they lack this form of capital. In other words, and reflecting on the connections between SDG4 and SDG8, there is no alternative to ensuring inclusive and equitable schooling for enhanced future social and economic futures. For this to happen, it is critical to examine what is misrecog- nised and ensure provisions to govern the misrecognition of English-in-education policy. Regarding theoretical implications, this study moved beyond Sen’s conceptu- alisation of development as freedom, providing a comprehensive understanding of development in the context of LEP. Much research overlooks the underpinning assumptions and the politics of social change and assumes development as a neutral process (e.g., Erling, 2017; Eyres et al., 2019). Reflecting our theoretical framework, we have highlighted that English and development ideologies in LEP and aid-based projects are highly political as they contribute to neoliberal governmentality. On that note, we have also shown the potential of the concept of misrecognition in LEP research from a social justice perspective. Building on existing theoretical perspec- tives around linguistic human capital, governmentality, and affect in language policy research (e.g., Ali & Hamid, 2020; De Costa et al., 2019; Highet, 2024; Park, 2011; Rojo & Del Percio, 2020), our study shows that Bourdieu’s concept of misrecogni- tion helps us move our understanding beyond neoliberal governmental rationalities and subjectivities in an affective regime. Misrecognition provides a critical lens to unpack how people from low SES contexts are marginalised through these govern- mental rationalities promoted through LEP. This includes how this system of oppres- sion is disguised through supposedly ‘neutral’ discourses of development. We have argued that recognising such lacunae is the first step towards a social justice agenda in language policy and education research in the context of development. This study, therefore, offers new perspectives to critique development ideology in relation to LEP in developing countries. Development ideologies in LEP are guided by human capital theory which constructs English language skills as valued human capital (Ali et al., 2023a). By presenting English language as a neutral tool for indi- vidual and social development, human capital theory contributes to the misrecogni- tion of the structural dominance of English. This is evident in the way the English in Action project construed £50 million aid as an investment in developing Bangladeshi poor people’s employability to graduate them out of poverty, without considering the role of the national and indigenous languages in such development (Ali et al., 2023a). At the same time, development ideologies promoted through the discourses of English and employability contribute to governing individuals’ habitus so they also misrecognise such politically/ideologically constructed linguistic hierarchies in accessing economic opportunities. As such, they construe English as a neutral tool for socioeconomic development. Reflecting Bourdieu’s theorising, this study particu- 1 3 1 Page 22 of 26 M. M. Ali et al. larly sheds light on how such misrecognition is deemed essential in the process of how English becomes an object of desire to neoliberal citizens and why they accept unequal social struggles over human capital development as natural. Hence, while they reproduce the neoliberal logic of individualisation and discourse of hard work and resilience, the reproduction is enabled through the process of misrecognition. From a macro perspective, the process of misrecognition is legitimised by LEP in relation to development ideologies. LEP promotes English, considering it human capital required to meet the demands of the employment market and the global econ- omy (see Tollefson (2002) for an analysis of how LEP works to legitimise linguistic hierarchy). In doing this, LEP contributes to the misrecognition of how linguistic hierarchy is created and legitimised through education, promoting the dominance of English. At the same time, by construing linguistic human capital development as a neutral process, LEP also contributes to the misrecognition of human and social con- ditions of marginalised peoples for whom the visible object of desire for development masks invisible sufferings and an unequal race for linguistic human capital. Conclusion This article has emphasised the importance of considering human and social condi- tions of the lives of parents and students from low SES contexts in LEP research for human capital development. We have shown how language and education become objects of desire to the parents and students influenced by these objects, creating in them specific subjectivities and affect which guide them to accept dominant dis- courses as neutral, with the belief that success and/or failure to achieve these valued objects is an individual responsibility. We have argued that this system of governing people’s thoughts and behaviours may marginalise people from low SES contexts, particularly when social structures and people’s human and social conditions are misrecognised. We emphasise that development ideologies at the national level and aid-based English language programmes need to be subjected to critical scrutiny. While promoting neoliberal governmentality, aid-based programmes may contribute to exacerbating social inequalities by misrecognising social structures and how they influence human capital development. We have illustrated how affective desires for English are ideologically constructed in the context of development, which are also structurally constrained for people from low SES contexts. The human capital orien- tation to LEP misrecognises social structures and human and social conditions and how they shape human capital development in the school context. Our study makes an original contribution to language policy in education by offering new perspectives which critique development ideology in relation to LEP. We have emphasised that misrecognition is central to the process of how English becomes an ‘object of desire’ to neoliberal citizens and how unequal social struggles over linguistic human capital development are accepted as natural. In particular, our analysis has shed light on how such misrecognition is operationalised and legitimised by human capital theory, development ideologies, and LEP. However, we acknowledge that the findings are contextually grounded in relation to a developing country and may not be generalised 1 3 Governmental rationalities and misrecognising human and social… Page 23 of 26 1 to other polities. Therefore, we would invite more research in this area in relation to other developing societies. Declarations Conflict of interest The authors declare that they have no conflict of interest. JSON: Name: lep_misrecognition_trial Title: Cluster randomized mixed-methods trial testing whether an awareness-plus-resource intervention reduces misrecognition of structural barriers and improves English linguistic human capital and school engagement in low-SES Bangladeshi secondary schools Short Hypothesis: Delivering a combined intervention of structural-barriers awareness training for parents and students plus school-level resource support will cause a greater reduction in parental/student self-blame and a greater increase in students' English proficiency and school engagement relative to business-as-usual. Related Work: Existing literature frames English-in-education policy in developing contexts through human capital theory, governmentality, affective economies, and misrecognition, and reports qualitative case studies showing affect-driven desire for English and structural barriers that mediate outcomes. Prior empirical work is predominantly descriptive and qualitative, documenting associations between neoliberal policy discourses and learner/parent dispositions but rarely testing causal mechanisms. Intervention studies that exist focus on large-scale media/teacher-training campaigns or tutoring programs without isolating the role of changing structural-awareness or affective dispositions; they typically lack randomized designs, validated quantitative measures of misrecognition/self-blame, and component-level comparisons. Limitations in current approaches include weak causal identification, limited measurement of affective and ideological constructs, scarcity of mixed-methods trials that link changes in dispositions to measurable learning outcomes, and little evidence on scalability and the comparative efficacy of awareness versus material supports. Abstract: Problem: Language-in-education policies that promote English as human capital can generate affective desires while misrecognising structural barriers faced by low-SES populations, potentially perpetuating inequality. Approach: We propose a cluster randomized mixed-methods trial in low-SES Bangladeshi secondary schools to test whether a two-component intervention—(A) structured awareness training for parents and students about structural determinants of learning and (B) targeted school-level resource supports (supplemental tutoring and midday nutrition)—reduces misrecognition (measured as self-blame) and improves English proficiency and engagement. Main contribution: The study provides the first randomized causal test linking reduced misrecognition to measurable gains in linguistic human capital, and uses a componential (ablation) design to separate the effects of awareness and resources. Expected outcome: Evidence whether changing structural-awareness and/or providing resources causally alters affective dispositions and produces measurable improvements in English learning and school participation; results will inform equitable LEP implementation and policy design. Experiments: Design: Cluster randomized controlled trial with four arms: (1) Control (business-as-usual LEP), (2) Awareness-only (A), (3) Resource-only (B), (4) Combined (A+B). Clusters: 40 secondary schools in comparable low-SES hill-tract communities, randomized 10 schools per arm. Participants: ~50 students per school in Grades 9–10 (N≈2000 students) and one primary parent/guardian per student. Timeline: Baseline, 6-month midpoint, 12-month endline. Datasets and measures: 1) Student-level demographics and household SES survey; 2) English proficiency: locally validated standardized English test aligned to national curriculum (pre/post); 3) Self-Blame Scale (validated/adapted and psychometrically tested in pilot) and Structural-Awareness Scale; 4) School engagement: attendance logs, homework completion rates, class participation scores; 5) Administrative outcomes: retention and pass rates; 6) Qualitative data: semi-structured interviews and focus groups with purposive subsample (n≈80 students, n≈40 parents, n≈20 teachers across arms). Baselines: business-as-usual and any existing remedial programs recorded. Ablation: compare A vs B vs A+B vs control to isolate component effects. Analysis: intention-to-treat hierarchical linear mixed-effects models with random intercepts for school and fixed effects for time and arm; primary outcomes: change in English proficiency score and change in Self-Blame Scale at 12 months. Secondary analyses: mediation analysis testing whether reduction in self-blame mediates proficiency/engagement gains; subgroup analyses by baseline SES, gender, and baseline language exposure; robustness checks with multiple imputation for missing data and cluster-robust standard errors; qualitative thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke procedure) to triangulate mechanisms. Power: with ICC=0.05 and 10 schools/arm and 50 students/school, the design detects effect size d≈0.25–0.30 on student-level outcomes at 80% power. Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Contamination: information spillover between arms in geographically proximate communities could bias effect estimates. 2) Noncompliance and differential uptake: parents/students may not attend awareness sessions or use resource supports, reducing observed effect sizes and complicating ITT interpretation. 3) Measurement validity: self-blame and structural-awareness scales may not fully capture local idioms or may be susceptible to social desirability bias. 4) Short follow-up: 12 months may be insufficient to observe durable changes in linguistic capital that affect employment outcomes. 5) External validity: findings from a specific indigenous low-SES Bangladeshi region may not generalize to other linguistic, cultural or national contexts. 6) Ethical constraints: withholding material supports from control schools raises equity concerns and may limit feasible experimental contrasts. 7) Implementation fidelity: variability in tutor quality, nutrition delivery, or facilitator performance could introduce heterogeneity and reduce interpretability. 8) Resource intensity: combined interventions may be costly, limiting scalability even if effective. 9) Data biases: administrative records (attendance, homework) may be incomplete or manipulated. 10) Unintended effects: raising structural-awareness could increase frustration or reduce short-term motivation if not paired with tangible supports.
